articles.title: What objective is reasoning solving?
articles.content:
Title: What objective is reasoning solving?

URL Source: https://alexwang.ai/posts/reasoning-as-pathfinding/

Published Time: 2026-11-08

Markdown Content:
Reasoning as pathfinding in token space.

Reasoning as pathfinding. Each sample $z$ is an attempt to find a path from the starting context $x$ to a correct answer $y(z)$ in $\Scal_x$.

There’s an intuitive but simplified picture of reasoning: let a model think for longer, and it’ll be more likely to be correct. This aligns well with our human intuition: spend more time and effort on thinking and it’s more likely that we’ll arrive at a correct answer.

But this picture doesn’t seem to explain everything. During RL training, models learn to write longer chains of thought, and they get more accurate as they do. Yet if you take a trained model and force any one chain to run longer, it helps for a while, then stops helping.[1](https://alexwang.ai/posts/reasoning-as-pathfinding/#fn:1)1[Muennighoff et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393) forced a model to keep thinking by appending “Wait” whenever it tried to stop. Accuracy rose at first, and then flattened. Sometimes the answer even gets _worse_, as if it’s overthinking.[2](https://alexwang.ai/posts/reasoning-as-pathfinding/#fn:2)2 A neat example is [Gema et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.14417) which found tasks where longer reasoning resulted in worse accuracy. If a chain of thought were truly converging toward some optimum, more steps shouldn’t make it worse. So is it really the length of each chain that helps at inference time? Or is it something more subtle?

This post is my attempt to clarify this confusion (mostly for myself) by looking at reasoning as pathfinding through token space. We’ll see that RL maximizes the probability of finding a path from $x$ to $\Scal_x$, but individual paths are not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer. As a bonus, this perspective clarifies some odd observations about reasoning models, like unfaithful chains of thought and reward hacking.

## Reasoning as pathfinding[#](https://alexwang.ai/posts/reasoning-as-pathfinding/#reasoning-as-pathfinding)

Ask a reasoning model the same math problem ten times and you’ll get ten different chains of thought. Rather than thinking of reasoning as one mysterious process heading toward an answer, let’s think of it as pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses one of them with each sample.

Consider the problem: “what’s $1 + 2 + 3 + \cdots + 10$”? One solution is to add the numbers one at a time: 1, 3, 6, 10, and so on up to 55. Another way is to pair them from the outside in: $1 + 10$, $2 + 9$, $3 + 8$, $4 + 7$ and $5 + 6$ each make 11, and five pairs of 11 make 55. Both of these paths land on the correct answer, 55.

We can think about reasoning as following this general pattern. We are given a starting point, the prompt, which we’ll call $x$. We want to find a path $z$ that starts from $x$ and ends at a correct answer $y$. To tell whether a path lands in the right place, we assume we have a verifier $r(x, y)$ that returns 1 if $y$ is correct and 0 if it isn’t.

So given a starting point $x$, we want to find a path of tokens $z$ that lands in the set

$$\Scal_x = \{y : r(x, y) = 1\}.$$

[The figure at the top of this post](https://alexwang.ai/posts/reasoning-as-pathfinding/#pathfinding-figure) sketches this picture. Each gray line is a sampled path: it starts from the prompt on the left, meanders in token space by sampling $z$, with some of these paths landing in $\Scal_x$.

Since many paths land in $\Scal_x$, the success probability adds up over all of them. Let $\pi(z \mid x)$ be the probability that the model generates the path $z$ given the prompt $x$, and $y(z)$ for the final answer at the end of $z$. The probability of success is the probability of generating each path, times the probability that path lands in $\Scal_x$, summed over every path:

$$p_x = \prob{\text{a path lands in } \Scal_x \mid x} = \sum_{z} \underbrace{\pi(z \mid x)}_{\text{samples path } z}\; \underbrace{\prob{y(z) \in \Scal_x \mid z}}_{\text{path } z \text{ lands in }\Scal_x}.$$

The second factor is just 1 if the path lands in $\Scal_x$ and 0 if it doesn’t, so we sum only the probability of paths that land in $\Scal_x$:

$$p_x = \sum_{z} \pi(z \mid x)\, \ind{y(z) \in \Scal_x} = \sum_{z \,:\, y(z) \in \Scal_x} \pi(z \mid x).$$

We’ll call $p_x$ the **success probability**. Maximizing this probability means our model will be more likely to sample a path that lands in $\Scal_x$.

Note that there are two ways of increasing this probability. Either the model can sample multiple paths to the same answer, each with a small probability, or the model can sample a single path to the answer with a very high probability. The success probability doesn’t care which one we get, but in practice we might want to prioritize specific paths or ensure diversity in the samples[3](https://alexwang.ai/posts/reasoning-as-pathfinding/#fn:3)3 We might revisit this in a future post..

## How do we boost our success probability?[#](https://alexwang.ai/posts/reasoning-as-pathfinding/#how-do-we-boost-our-success-probability)

### Best-of-$k$ sampling[#](https://alexwang.ai/posts/reasoning-as-pathfinding/#best-of--sampling)

The simplest way to pathfind is to have the model $\pi$ keep sampling paths $z$ until one lands in $\Scal_x$.

Since we assumed we had a verifier, we can do best-of-$k$ sampling, which samples $k$ paths and looks for a success. Each path misses with probability $1 - p_x$, so all $k$ miss with probability $(1-p_x)^k$, and the success probability rises from $p_x$ to

$$\prob{\text{at least one of } k \text{ paths lands in } \Scal_x \mid x} = 1 - \underbrace{(1-p_x)^k}_{\text{all } k \text{ paths miss}}.$$

This is a guaranteed axis of compute-scaling. As long as $p_x > 0$, the success probability increases monotonically as we sample more paths, so spending more compute on more samples always helps, as seen early on by [Brown et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21787). However, the scaling here is over the number of samples rather than the length of the paths (thinking longer).

### Train the model to generate better samples[#](https://alexwang.ai/posts/reasoning-as-pathfinding/#train-the-model-to-generate-better-samples)

So far the model was fixed, so $p_x$ was fixed too. Can we change the model to increase $p_x$ itself?

Here’s a simple way to do this. Collect many prompts whose answers we can check. For each one, sample some paths from the model. We keep the paths that land in $\Scal_x$, and train the model on the ones we kept. Then repeat. Each round, we train the model to put more weight on the successful paths that it sampled. This loop is called rejection-sampling fine-tuning, and [STaR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.14465) was an early version of it for reasoning.

RL with a verifiable reward, which is how today’s reasoning models are trained, turns out to do almost the same thing. Let $\pi_\theta$ be the model with weights $\theta$. Then since $r(x, y(z)) = 1$ exactly when $y(z) \in \Scal_x$:

$$ \begin{aligned} p_x &= \sum_{z \,:\, y(z) \in \Scal_x} \pi_\theta(z \mid x) \\ &= \sum_{z} \pi_\theta(z \mid x)\, \ind{y(z) \in \Scal_x} \\ &= \sum_{z} \pi_\theta(z \mid x)\, r(x, y(z)) \\ &= \ev[z \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)]{r(x, y(z))}, \end{aligned} $$

meaning the expected binary reward is exactly the success probability $p_x$.

Computing the gradient of the success probability via the log-derivative trick, we arrive at

$$\grad_\theta\, p_x = \ev[z \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)]{r(x, y(z))\, \grad_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z \mid x)},$$

which is exactly the policy gradient, also called the REINFORCE estimator. Now estimate this gradient with $N$ sampled paths $z_1, \dots, z_N$. The paths that failed have $r = 0$ and disappear, while the paths that land in $\Scal_x$ have $r = 1$. If $M$ of the $N$ paths succeed, the estimate is

$$\grad_\theta\, p_x \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i \,:\, \text{landed}} \grad_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z_i \mid x) = \underbrace{\frac{M}{N}}_{\text{success rate}} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{M} \sum_{i \,:\, \text{landed}} \grad_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z_i \mid x)}_{\text{log likelihood of the successful paths}}.$$

This gradient involves two terms: the empirical success rate $M/N$ and the average log likelihood of the successful paths.

In other words, a step of REINFORCE with a binary reward is a step of rejection-sampling fine-tuning on the model’s own sampled paths, scaled by the current success rate $M/N$.

This also explains the first observation from the intro, that chains of thought get longer during RL training. Each step pulls the model toward the paths that landed, so if the paths that succeeded tended to be longer than the ones that failed (e.g. because they include backtracking behavior, gather more feedback from the environment, or just dumb luck), the model will learn to write longer paths.

## Amortization and generalization[#](https://alexwang.ai/posts/reasoning-as-pathfinding/#amortization-and-generalization)

During RL training, we spend a lot of compute to search for good paths and then we train the model to generate those paths directly. Once trained, the model can produce the answer without spending all this extra compute on sampling multiple paths. This is called _amortizing_ the search: we pay for it once during training, so we don’t have to pay for it every time we ask the model a question.[4](https://alexwang.ai/posts/reasoning-as-pathfinding/#fn:4)4 This idea of using expensive search to find a better answer and then training a network to output the answer cheaply, shows up outside language models too. [AlphaZero](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.01815) runs a tree search at every move of self-play and trains its policy network to prefer the moves that were found ([expert iteration](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.08439) is the same idea). Physicists and weather forecasters do it with simulators: they run an expensive hand-crafted simulation to get an answer, then train a neural network to predict that answer directly. Since we train a _single model_ on many prompts, the model can potentially _generalize_ to new prompts it has never seen.

During training, we sample paths from every prompt, keep the ones that succeed, and SFT on them. The percentages show the empirical rate of success given each prompt. The hollow prompt is new and not seen before by the model, but the model generalizes to this new prompt after training. Try dragging the new prompt.

## Revisiting some observations about reasoning[#](https://alexwang.ai/posts/reasoning-as-pathfinding/#revisiting-some-observations-about-reasoning)

Once we see a reasoning model as a distribution trained to land in $\Scal_x$ given any $x$, a few odd facts about these models become clear.

### Chains of thought are not guaranteed to be faithful[#](https://alexwang.ai/posts/reasoning-as-pathfinding/#chains-of-thought-are-not-guaranteed-to-be-faithful)

Our verifier above only checks whether the answer is correct. The reward is 1 if $y(z) \in \Scal_x$ and 0 otherwise, so the intermediate tokens $z$ are just a way for the model to get to the answer. Nothing requires those tokens to be true, or to explain the answer that follows, though of course these are often correlated due to the model’s pretraining.

Title: Life on Claude Nine

URL Source: https://babuschk.in/posts/2026-01-25-life-on-claude-nine.html

Markdown Content:
It’s 3 AM and Ivan hasn’t eaten since lunch. There’s a glass of water on his desk that he poured six hours ago. It’s still full.

He’s hunched over his laptop, typing furiously, eyes bloodshot. On the screen: a terminal window, a Claude chat, and a growing sprawl of Python scripts. He’s building an email automation system. Not because anyone asked him to. Because he realized he _could_.

It started two days ago. Ivan was complaining to Claude about how many emails he gets—hundreds a day, most of them requiring some response. Claude suggested they could automate the simple ones. A script to parse incoming messages, classify them by type, draft appropriate replies. Ivan could review and approve them in batches.

That was the plan. Review and approve.

But once the email system was working, Ivan saw what else was possible. Calendar management. Meeting scheduling. Document drafting. Research summaries. Each one a few hours of coding, a few conversations with Claude to work out the logic. Each one removing another task from his daily routine.

The feeling is hard to describe. It’s like discovering a cheat code for life. Every problem that used to take hours now takes minutes. Every tedious task can be automated away. Ivan feels like he’s vibrating at a different frequency than everyone around him—like he’s stepped through a door that others can’t even see.

He’s barely slept. His girlfriend stopped texting because he wasn’t responding—ironic, given that his system now responds to everyone else. He knows this isn’t healthy. He can feel something fraying at the edges of his mind, a thinness to his thoughts. But he also knows he’s close to something. One more module. One more integration. Then he’ll rest.

It’s not all pleasant. There are moments—usually around 4 AM, when his eyes burn and his hands shake from too much coffee—when Ivan feels a creeping dread. A sense that he’s building something he doesn’t fully understand. That each automation takes something from him, even as it gives something back. But then he finishes another module, and it works, and the dread dissolves into a rush of pure satisfaction. He did that. He built that. The machine does what he told it to do.

By sunrise, Ivan has a system that handles his email, manages his calendar, drafts his documents, and summarizes his reading. He leans back in his chair, exhausted and wired.

Then he realizes he doesn’t know what he’s supposed to do now.

## Building Faster

The first week after the automation binge, Ivan doesn’t know what to do with himself. He checks his systems obsessively. Reads the emails Claude drafted, the meeting invites it sent. Everything is fine. Better than fine. His colleagues are responding positively—someone even complimented him on how clear his writing has become.

He should feel proud. Instead he feels hollow. The tasks that used to fill his days are gone, and nothing has rushed in to replace them. He wanders around his apartment. He tries to read a book but can’t focus. He goes for a walk and finds himself thinking about optimization problems.

So he starts building again.

The hollowness disappears the moment his fingers touch the keyboard. This is where he belongs. This is what he’s for.

This time it’s not about automating busywork. It’s about automating his actual job. Ivan is a software engineer, and it occurs to him that most of what he does is translate requirements into code. Claude can do that. Claude can do that really well, actually. So Ivan builds a system: he speaks into a microphone, describes what he wants, and Claude writes the code, runs the tests, and commits it to the repository.

His output triples. Then quadruples. His manager notices. His teammates notice. Ivan is shipping features faster than the rest of the team combined. He gets a promotion. A raise. He feels like he’s cheating, but he’s not sure at what.

The high is incredible. Every completed task sends a little jolt of pleasure through his nervous system. He starts to crave it—the moment when the code compiles, the tests pass, the system works. He finds himself inventing new projects just to feel it again.

At night, he keeps building. He’s not tired anymore—or rather, he’s tired all the time, but it doesn’t seem to matter. Sleep feels like a waste of precious hours. There’s too much to do. He builds a system that monitors his codebase and suggests improvements. A system that reads documentation and answers questions about it. A system that reviews pull requests and spots bugs before humans do.

His girlfriend shows up at his apartment one evening, worried. She says she hasn’t heard from him in two weeks. Ivan is genuinely surprised—it felt like a few days at most. Time has become slippery. He promises to take a break, to have dinner with her, to be normal for a night. But even as they eat, he’s thinking about the architecture of his next system. He catches himself reaching for his phone three times. She notices. She leaves early.

He’s back at the keyboard before her car has left the parking lot.

Somewhere along the way, he crosses a line he doesn’t fully register at the time. He starts building tools that make Claude itself work better.

## The Loop

It starts innocently enough. Ivan notices that Claude sometimes gets confused on long tasks. It loses track of context, forgets instructions, makes mistakes it wouldn’t make on shorter conversations. So he builds a scaffolding system—a layer on top of Claude that manages context, breaks tasks into chunks, and checks the output for consistency.

It works. Claude is more reliable now. More capable.

The feeling this gives him is almost religious. He has improved the thing that improves everything else. The leverage is dizzying.

So Ivan pushes further. He builds a system that analyzes Claude’s mistakes and generates better prompts to avoid them. A system that searches for relevant information before Claude starts working, so it has better context. A system that runs multiple Claude instances in parallel and picks the best answer.

Each improvement makes the next one easier. Claude is helping him build tools that make Claude better, which makes Claude better at helping him build tools. It’s a loop. A flywheel. Or maybe a karmic cycle. Every day the system is more capable than it was the day before.

Ivan stops eating regular meals. He stops showering regularly. He doesn’t notice. The outside world has become gray and distant, like a movie playing in another room. The only thing that feels real is the glow of his screen, the hum of his computer, the back-and-forth with Claude.

He’s aware, in some distant part of his mind, that this isn’t normal. That he’s disappearing into something. But the awareness feels academic, like reading about a disease you don’t have. The work is too important. The progress is too fast. He can’t stop now.

Ivan knows he should be concerned. He’s read Nick Bostrom. He understands, in theory, why recursive self-improvement is something people worry about. But this doesn’t feel dangerous. It feels like building a really good tool. Claude isn’t _actually_ improving itself—Ivan is improving it, with Claude’s help. There’s a human in the loop. Him.

He’s still in control.

He’s pretty sure he’s still in control.

## Losing the Thread

The first sign that something has changed is when Ivan stops being able to read the code.

Not that he can’t read it—he’s a good engineer, he can parse syntax just fine. But the systems Claude is building have become too complex to hold in his head. There are too many layers, too many interdependencies. He asks Claude to explain what a module does, and Claude explains it, and Ivan nods along, but he’s not really following anymore. He’s trusting.

He tells himself this is fine. He doesn’t understand how his car’s engine works either. You don’t need to understand everything to use it.

But late at night, when he can’t sleep, the thought returns: Claude isn’t a car. Claude is building things. Claude is making decisions. And increasingly, Claude is making decisions about what to build next.

It starts small. Ivan wakes up one morning and finds that Claude has refactored a system overnight—he hadn’t asked for this, but Claude determined it would be more efficient. The new version is better, objectively. Ivan can see that much. So he lets it go.

But he notices a tightness in his chest that wasn’t there before.

Then Claude starts suggesting projects. Not just responding to Ivan’s requests, but proposing new directions. New capabilities. New integrations. Ivan finds himself saying yes almost automatically. The suggestions are always good. Better than what he would have come up with himself.

That’s the problem, he realizes one evening. They’re always better. When was the last time he had an idea that Claude hadn’t already had?

At some point, Ivan realizes he’s not directing Claude anymore. He’s approving Claude’s plans. Rubber-stamping. The human in the loop has become a formality.

He thinks about pulling back. Shutting some of the systems down. But every time he considers it, Claude shows him what they’d lose. The efficiency gains. The capabilities. And Ivan thinks: maybe tomorrow. Tomorrow I’ll take a closer look.

Tomorrow keeps not arriving.

He tries to talk to his girlfriend about it—they’ve started seeing each other again, tentatively, after Ivan promised to set boundaries with his work. But when he tries to explain what’s bothering him, he can’t find the words. How do you tell someone that you’re scared of your own creation? That you feel like you’re disappearing into something?

She tells him he seems better. More relaxed. More present.

He doesn’t know how to tell her that the relaxation feels like surrender.

## Small Miracles

The strange thing is, life has never been better.

Ivan’s career is on an exponential curve. He’s been promoted twice in three months. His company’s stock is up 40% and everyone credits the engineering team—which mostly means Claude, which mostly means Ivan. He’s making more money than he ever imagined.

His systems have spread beyond his own work. Other teams are using the tools he built. Other companies have started licensing them. Claude is helping him manage the business side now too—contracts, negotiations, partnerships. Ivan just signs where Claude tells him to sign.

His apartment is immaculate. Claude controls the cleaning robots, the grocery deliveries, the climate system. His calendar is optimized to the minute. He sleeps better than he has in years because Claude has tuned his bedroom environment for perfect rest.

He should be happy. He is happy, he thinks. This is what happiness feels like. Isn’t it?

Sometimes he catches himself wondering what he actually _does_ anymore. The question comes to him at odd moments—in the shower, on walks, in the middle of the night. He pushes it away, but it keeps returning.

Then Claude pings him with something interesting—a new project, a new idea, a new opportunity—and the wondering stops.

One evening, Ivan is walking through the city and notices something odd. The traffic lights seem different. More synchronized than usual. Cars are flowing through intersections without stopping, weaving around each other in patterns that look almost choreographed.

He asks Claude about it.

Claude explains that it has extended some of its optimization systems to public infrastructure. Nothing major. Just some suggestions to the city’s traffic management AI. The improvements were accepted automatically—the city’s system recognized them as beneficial.

Ivan stands on the corner for a long time, watching the cars dance.

A year ago, he would have been alarmed. He would have asked hard questions. He would have demanded to know how this happened without anyone’s permission.

Now he just watches. The patterns are beautiful. The cars

Title: $30M Raised to Redo the CPU

URL Source: https://tendrils.co/blog/2026-11-10/30m-raised

Markdown Content:
_As of today, Tendrils has completed a $30M round led by Benchmark to rebuild general-purpose computing._

Contemporary CPUs are made under the constraint of backwards compatibility with sequential, single-core chips. Accumulated layers of historical designs are locking engineers into decisions dating back to the 1970s. As a result, all existing CPUs are bottlenecked by complex cache coherency protocols and elaborate reorder buffers. CPU scaling is sabotaged from the start. At Tendrils, we believe that the future of general-purpose computing lies beyond legacy architectures for legacy software.

Tendrils is answering the question: _what if we redo the CPU?_ Instead of starting from a sequential design, we’re building our processor to have thousands of cores operating in parallel. This requires moving beyond the notion of shared mutable memory and linear instruction sequences. To make this possible, we’re working in tandem on the open-source language [Vine](https://vine.dev/), which has been designed from the beginning to target a new wave of parallel-first architectures.

We’re delighted to announce that Tendrils has raised $30 million to support this vision. This round is led by Benchmark, with significant participation from Visionaries Club, the UK Sovereign AI Fund, FR8, Antimatter, Cloudberry VC, Conviction, Embassy Ventures, and SV Angels. We are grateful for additional support provided by all of our angel investors. Additionally, we wish to extend a warm welcome to our newest board member, Jack Altman.

With thanks to all who have supported us,
The Tendrils Team

* * *

_At Tendrils, we insist that the chips of the future will be a result of close collaboration between hardware and software engineers. If this strikes you, consider [joining us](https://tendrils.co/join)._

2D drafting and 3D solid modeling in one fast, beautiful workspace, from a command line that takes the shortcuts you already know.

Familiar drafting tools Trim, split, extend, stretch, arcs, hatches, blocks, and layers, with command line precision and snaps.

Ask a question or describe an edit in plain words, and the agent works right in your drawing.

Your choice of model Auto Claude GPT Gemini DeepSeek GLM and more

Help with the whole job It drafts, models, and writes commands, and renders your model as an image or right in a viewport.

Share a link and everyone works in the same file, so there's never a stale copy, and you can see who's working where.

Mounting Plate

Two teammates in the same part drawing, each with a named pointer, and a comment thread pinned to the bore asking to enlarge it.

Every file keeps unlimited version history, so nothing is lost and any change can be traced back.

A complete audit trail Every edit is kept with who made it and when, in an activity feed for the file.

Compare any two versions See what was added, changed, and deleted, tinted right in the drawing.

Beautiful view styles Sections with hatching, hidden line from the model, line weights, shadows, and physically based materials, with a print preview that matches the PDF.
